This document provides a detailed overview of the headless, offline video rendering pipeline implemented for **Retiam**, a WebGPU-powered animation engine. It outlines the architectural design, configuration options, usage patterns, and industrial use cases.

Traditional web rendering loops rely on `requestAnimationFrame` and real-world system clocks (`performance.now()`). While this works for interactive, real-time web applications, it introduces non-determinism during offline video export. Variable CPU/GPU loads cause frame drops, stuttering, and inconsistent rendering results.
The Retiam offline rendering pipeline completely decouples simulation time from wall-clock time, ensuring frame-perfect, deterministic video generation.

items: **Programmatic Dev Server (Vite)**: The Node.js execution engine (`render.js`) starts a local, programmatic Vite server. If the default port (`5173`) is occupied, it automatically shifts to the next available port, preventing conflicts.

**Headless Browser (Puppeteer)**: The script launches a headless instance of Chromium with flags enabled for unsafe WebGPU configurations (`--enable-unsafe-webgpu`). It navigates to the compiled local URL while passing render variables via query parameters (e.g., `?offline=true&width=1920&height=1080&fps=60`).

**Deterministic Canvas Stepper (Browser)**: The engine detects the `offline=true` parameter. It cancels the standard `requestAnimationFrame` loop, locks `renderring = true`, and runs an explicit step loop. Time advances by a fixed interval (`1000 / FPS`) per frame.

**WebSocket Coordination & Backpressure**: For every frame, the browser converts the WebGPU canvas into an image blob and transmits it to Node.js over a local WebSocket. The browser halts execution and waits for a WebSocket acknowledgment (`"ack"`) from Node.js before rendering the next frame. This prevents browser memory exhaustion.

**Muxing (FFmpeg)**: Node.js receives the binary frame and writes it directly to the writable standard input (`stdin`) of an active FFmpeg subprocess. When the animation queue is empty, the browser signals a `"finish"` event, closing the FFmpeg pipe and writing the final MP4 or WebM video file.

blocks.text: When Raytracing is enabled, WebGPU requires multiple render passes over multiple sub-frames (accumulation) to denoise the output. During offline rendering, Retiam freezes the simulation clock, sets motion indicators to false, and loops the WebGPU `capture` routine for `rtMaxAccumulation` iterations before extracting the frame. The resulting frame is fully accumulated, denoised, and exported before the simulation clock progresses to the next step.

blocks.text: Because the pipeline runs headlessly and deterministically in headless environments, it can be integrated into CI/CD pipelines (e.g., GitHub Actions) to regenerate documentation assets, math visualizers, or UI promotional videos automatically whenever code changes are pushed to a repository.

For complex scenes or high-resolution raytracing, rendering locally can be slow. Since the pipeline is triggered via a CLI wrapper, you can deploy your project to a cloud container (e.g., Docker running on AWS or Google Cloud). The container can spin up Node.js, run Chromium with WebGPU headless flags, compile the scene, and render the output using the cloud instance's resources.

For research papers, scientific displays, or financial data visualizations, you can feed a JSON dataset to the engine. The CLI can render deterministic, high-fidelity 3D graphs, streamlines, vector fields, or math animations on-the-fly and output customized, polished video files for presentations.
